entries.title: MineralExp: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Experimental Design in Real-World Mineral Exploration
entries.abstract: In mineral exploration, verifying geological hypotheses relies on designing a variety of geochemical experiments. While large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate downstream geoscientific data analysis, a crucial upstream capability remains largely unexplored: automated geochemical experimental design, i.e., deciding which experiments to conduct before committing to costly laboratory work. Evaluating this capability of LLM agents is difficult for two reasons. First, geochemical experiments exhibit high methodological diversity and subjectivity: to test the same hypothesis, different geologists may choose different minerals and instruments, so no single protocol can serve as the reference answer. Second, open-ended experimental plans resist representation as structured labels, which makes objective scoring difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce MineralExp, a benchmark that reformulates geochemical experimental design as a hypothesis-based experiment selection problem, i.e., a multi-label classification problem. We abstract concrete instrument names and procedural details into a shared taxonomy of 19 experimental types across five mineral-system processes: Source, Transport, Deposition, Modification, and Preservation. This taxonomy yields deterministic multi-label targets while accommodating diverse experimental protocols. Constructed from published ore-deposit literature and verified by domain experts, MineralExp comprises 277 cases and 1,572 reference experimental plans. Given a geological hypothesis and initial context, an LLM agent selects the relevant tasks and generates concrete experimental plans, which are scored by multi-label classification metrics and an LLM-as-a-Judge metric. The experimental results show that current agents generally achieve high recall but low precision, tending to propose more experiments than are necessary to test the hypothesis.

entries.title: OpenMedEval: Benchmarking 172 open-source LLMs on 326K medical questions across 93 datasets.
entries.abstract: To address the practical challenges, including the difficulties in safeguarding medical data privacy arising from the closed-source nature of commercial large language models (LLMs), the limitations of existing benchmarks that predominantly focus on English-centric scenarios, and the inadequate consideration of deployment-related factors such as inference speed and parameter efficiency, we propose the OpenMedEval benchmark framework. This work aims to fill the gap in the systematic evaluation of open-source medical LLMs. The framework comprises 326,100 medical questions across 93 datasets, covering over 30 medical specialties and 4 professional tiers (ranging from entry-level licensing to senior specialist certification). It incorporates diverse assessment sources such as the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE), nephrology cases from the American Journal of Kidney Diseases (AJKD), and Chinese Medical Licensing Examinations spanning 2017-2024. We conduct multi-dimensional evaluations on 172 open-source models with parameter scales ranging from 0.5B to 671B, integrating deployment-relevant metrics including inference speed and instruction-following compliance. Experimental results demonstrate that reasoning-enhanced architectures (e.g., DeepSeek-R1, QWQ) outperform general-purpose models by 20-40 percentage points in accuracy. Specifically, DeepSeek-R1-70B achieves an average accuracy of 81.8% across all datasets and 97% on the USMLE. Model rankings are reported as a macro-average over the 93 datasets and are shown to be robust to the aggregation scheme (Spearman ρ=0.999 against question-weighted accuracy) and to language stratification (ρ=0.9998 against a Chinese-only ranking); because 99.9% of questions are Chinese-language, overall figures are Chinese-dominant and English results are reported separately. Parameter-efficient models (e.g., Phi4-Reasoning-14B) exhibit performance comparable to ultra-large-scale general-purpose counterparts. Additionally, inference speed varies by 2000× across different models. These findings provide guidance for the selection of open-source models tailored to diverse deployment scenarios, from real-time triage to complex diagnostic support. We present such scenarios as candidate applications implied by the measured accuracy-throughput trade-off, not as demonstrated clinical readiness: performance on medical licensing examinations evidences domain knowledge and structured reasoning capacity, and any use in patient care would require prospective clinical validation, safety assessment, and regulatory approval.
